messages.subject: Issue with stochastic indexing in 0.6-12
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks,

I work with hierarchical linear models to estimate abundance from a subset of imperfectly detected individuals within the population - i.e., capture-recapture and spatial-capture-recapture models. I'm trying to fit in nimble  a single-season spatial capture-recapture model originally written in JAGS, and have come across an issue with stochastic/dynamic indexing: I get an error about dynamic indexing, which I thought is accommodated in version 0.6-12? I've tried a workaround, but that doesn't work either,  so any help would be much appreciated. I'm using nimbleOptions(allowDynamicIndexing = TRUE,showCompilerOutput = TRUE). The issue is as follows:

If I try to model a inhomogeneous point process to describe variation in density, I get the following error "Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(code, constNames, indexNames, nimbleFunctionNames,  :

  getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse: dynamic indexing of constants is not allowed in grid[s[i], 1]. Try adding the dynamically-indexed constant as data instead (using the data argument of nimbleModel)." This was essentially exactly Dan Linden'squestion and post on 12/21/15 <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/nimble-users/dynamic$20index$20linden%7Csort:date/nimble-users/TUs5RCw193M/jcHCokxaBQAJ> with this part of his likelihood:

> > >
> > > s[i]~dcat(probs[1:nG])
> > >
> > > d2[i,j]<- (grid[s[i],1]-grid[traps[j],1])^2 + (grid[s[i],2]-grid[traps[j],2])^2

So, I tried to implement Perry's recommendation in that thread to use a custom nimbleFunction (see below) to do the the indexing, and the model then successfully defined. Yay!

> > > myIndexCalc <- nimbleFunction(
> > >
> > >   run = function(gridCol = double(1), index = double()) {
> > >
> > >     return(gridCol [index])
> > >
> > >     returnType(double(0))
> > >
> > >   })

However, then I get a compiling error about an issue with 'sum' and 'non-class type 'double'', and then that the shared library is not created:
> > >
> > > compiling... this may take a minute. On some systems there may be some compiler warnings that can be safely ignored.

> > >
> > > c:/Rtools/mingw_64/bin/g++  -I"C:/PROGRA~1/R/R-35~1.1/include" -DNDEBUG -DR_NO_REMAP -I"C:/Users/CatSun/Documents/R/win-library/3.5/nimble/include" -I"" -I"" -DEIGEN_MPL2_ONLY=1 -Wno-misleading-indentation -Wno-ignored-attributes -Wno-deprecated-declarations         -O2 -Wall  -mtune=generic -c P_3_nimMod_SCR_MID_10_nfCode.cpp -o P_3_nimMod_SCR_MID_10_nfCode.o
> > >
> > > P_3_nimMod_SCR_MID_10_nfCode.cpp: In member function 'virtual void zi_L22_UID_43::simulate(const indexedNodeInfo&) const':
> > >
> > > P_3_nimMod_SCR_MID_10_nfCode.cpp:2509:65: error: request for member 'sum' in '(*(NimArr<1, double>**)((const zi_L22_UID_43*)this)->zi_L22_UID_43::model_z)->NimArr<1, double>::<anonymous>.NimArrBase<T>::operator[]<double>((int)((double)*ARG1_INDEXEDNODEINFO__->indexedNodeInfo::info.std::vector<double, std::allocator<double> >::operator[]()(0ull) - 1.0e+0))', which is of non-class type 'double'
> > >

messages.body_plain:
hi Cat,

You have the line:
zi[i] <- (sum(z[i]) > 0)

When we compile that to the C++ version of the model, z[i] is a scalar
and the sum function that is used in C++ expects a vector, matrix,
etc.

I suspect that you don't really want sum(z[i]) any way...

Chris

and similarly for y0g[i].

Chris

I have a follow up question about this. My data is one count for each week over a few years i.e. t=1,2,...,N.

Have any of you experienced this kind of problem before? Does anybody have a suggestion for the priors or an alternative formulation so that I can have a smooth but distinct temporal and seasonal component?

Best wishes,

Oliver

messages.subject: Re: configureMCMC
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gil,

A few thoughts here:

1) You should be able to configure the MCMC while allowing for
conjugate samplers here. What I did to get this to work was to move
'numid' from 'data' into 'constants'. I'm still diagnosing this, but
it seems to be that when the IDs are in 'data', they are not regarded
as fixed and so NIMBLE ends up thinking that every observation is a
dependency of every random effect and this slows down the conjugacy
checking (and would slow down any sampling as well). Since you don't
have random indexes, they should just go in 'constants' so NIMBLE sees
that each random effect is tied to a small number of observations.

2) Once I do that I can get a basic MCMC using the default MCMC
configuration to run reasonably quickly per iteration (but mixing is
slow).

3) I see you are using the AF_slice sampler. However you are applying
it to vectors that have 2700-odd parameters and the AF_slice sampler
does a bunch of matrix calculations with matrices of size 2700 x 2700.
So I think that is why your sampling is very slow. I would suggest
trying to make smaller blocks of parameters that block together only
parameters that are highly correlated.

4) This may well not help mixing, since slow mixing is probably
because of parameter correlation across the levels of the hierarchy,
but if you use either a gamma prior on the precision of random effects
or an invgamma prior on the variance of the random effects (and in
that case, you need to specify the parameter directly using "var=" in
the dnorm() rather than as the precision with 1/variance_parameter),
you should get conjugate samplers for those parameters. Right now you
have a gamma prior on the variance, which is not conjugate.

Chris

messages.subject_clean: cross validation loss functions for binary response data
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to the developers and countless contributors for all the great work building this useful software.

Recently, I was using NIMBLE to fit Bayesian hierarchical models to binary response data (Pr(y_i = 1) = p_i), and I hoped to use the nimble::runCrossValidate() function to score various models and inform model selection. However, the class of loss functions that are definable by the user are limited to those that are only a function of realizations from the posterior predictive distribution (simulatedDataValues). For the case of binary data, this means I can't construct a proper scoring rule. What I'd like to do is specify a loss function that uses draws from the posterior distribution of p_i, the probability of observing a success for the ith (withheld) datum, such as L(y_i, p_i) = (y_i - p_i)^2.

Right now, I can produce the k-fold CV scores by manually defining the holdout sets, fitting the model to the subsetted data, and scoring it with the posterior samples produced by NIMBLE. It would be great if I could use runCrossValidate() to manage all the bookkeeping for that.

Additionally, as mentioned above, the default loss function is not proper (see for example, Gneiting and Raftery 2007. "Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation"). In fact, it selects for degenerate models for binary data in which p_i = 0 or 1. For users who are not familiar with the notion of score propriety, this default might lead to the development invalid statistical methodology.

Thanks again for all the hard work. I hope this feature request is both realizable and helpful.

Henry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Henry,

Thanks for this suggestion and pointing out the limits of the current implementation.  The lossFunction was intended to provide a general hook to do whatever you need, but it didn't turn out to be all that flexible.

What I'd like to do is make a branch on GitHub with a quick prototype of something more flexible for you.  You could try it and we can see if it leads somewhere useful.

The somewhat tricky part is that alignment of say p[1]...p[n] with y[1]...y[n] is  model-specific.  A model might instead have p[2]...p[n+1] aligned with y[1]...y[n] for some quirky reason.  The foldFunction currently returns node names for the held-out nodes ("leaveOutNodes" in function calcCrossVal in the crossValidate.R source code).

A somewhat more general solution would be to allow foldFunction to return additional information, such as a set of nodes (p[1]...p[n] in your example) for which posterior values should also be passed to lossFunction.  That would mean the foldFunction would be somewhat more complicated, and you would have to provide your own foldFunction and lossFunction for a custom case.

A more completely general solution would be to allow a user to provide a lossFunction that takes as arguments the compiled model, the names of leaveOutNodes, and the entire posterior sample (or, to avoid a large copy, the MCMC from which the sample can be extracted).  (Currently, a lossFunction takes one row of the posterior at a time.) This would require someone writing a new lossFunction to do more manipulation to get what they want.

Do you have a preference for the first solution (narrower) or the second solution (more general)?  Or another suggestion on how you'd like to be able to use it?

-Perry
